**Key idea:** Combine pairwise distinctness with a widened array reduction and a feasible sum.

| Distinct values in 0..9 | Sum |
| --- | --- |
| Minimum: 0,1,2,3 | 6 |
| Example: 1,4,6,9 | 20 |
| Maximum: 6,7,8,9 | 30 |

### Explanation
The original title does not supply a length, domain, or target. This concrete instance uses four elements, values zero through nine, and a total of twenty. Four distinct integers in this domain can sum only between six and thirty; checking those bounds quickly detects impossible requirements. The cast inside the reduction widens each term before addition.

### Code
```systemverilog
class distinct_sum;
  rand bit [3:0] a[4];
  constraint legal_c {
    foreach (a[i]) a[i] inside {[0:9]};
    foreach (a[i]) foreach (a[j]) if (i < j) a[i] != a[j];
    a.sum() with (int'(item)) == 20;
  }
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
A narrow reduction may overflow before comparison, so casting only the completed sum is insufficient. Distinctness does not impose ordering. Bounds are necessary but not sufficient for arbitrary sparse domains: a sum inside the min/max interval may still be unreachable. Always check solver success.

### Follow-ups
If N values are selected from consecutive integers L..U, the minimum sum is N*L+N*(N-1)/2, and the maximum is N*U-N*(N-1)/2.

```systemverilog

  rand bit [4:0] slot[4];
  constraint distinct_c { unique {slot}; }
  function int unsigned base_addr(int unsigned i);
    return int'(slot[i]) * 32;
  endfunction
```

| Cycle after cat | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

```systemverilog
  cat |=> dog[*3:4]);

  cat |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
```

**Key idea:** A 100 MHz clock has a 10 ns period; with ±5% tolerance the acceptable interval is 9.5–10.5 ns.

| Successive rises | Period | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10, 20 ns | 10 ns | Pass |
| 20, 30.5 ns | 10.5 ns | Pass at boundary |
| 30.5, 41.1 ns | 10.6 ns | Fail |

### Explanation
Measure successive rising edges with realtime rather than integer time so fractional nanoseconds are retained. The first edge after reset initializes history and makes no comparison. EXPECTED specifies the nominal rising-edge period, not the half period. For the 100 MHz question, the frequency is fixed but no tolerance was given; this example explicitly chooses ±5%, which should be replaced by the design requirement.

### Code
```systemverilog
module period_checker(input logic clk, rst_n);
  timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
  parameter realtime EXPECTED = 10ns;
  realtime previous_edge, measured;
  bit history = 0;
  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) history = 0;
    else begin
      if (history) begin
        measured = $realtime - previous_edge;
        assert (measured >= 0.95*EXPECTED &&
                measured <= 1.05*EXPECTED)
          else $error("Bad period: %0t", measured);
      end
      previous_edge = $realtime;
      history = 1;
    end
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
A checker triggered only by clock edges cannot fail if the clock stops permanently. Use an independent reference-clock or timed watchdog for that case. Period alone says nothing about duty cycle: a 1 ns high and 9 ns low waveform still has a 10 ns period. X/Z clock transitions can also trigger edge-sensitive processes; establish a known-clock policy.

### Follow-ups
For 50% duty cycle verification, measure rising-to-falling and falling-to-rising intervals separately, each against its own tolerance.

**Key idea:** Define when the asynchronous expected period takes effect, then compare each interval with the expectation assigned to that interval.

| Event | Expected value | Checker action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Edge at 0 ns | 10 ns | Capture 10 ns |
| Config changes at 4 ns | 20 ns | Do not rewrite prior interval |
| Edge at 10 ns | 20 ns | Check prior 10 ns; capture 20 ns |
| Edge at 30 ns | 20 ns | Check 20 ns |

This example adopts a next-edge policy: the expected value captured at one rising edge applies to the interval ending at the following edge. A configuration update within an interval therefore affects the next complete interval. This is a verification contract, not a physical synchronizer. The environment must make the value stable around the sampling edge, or provide a mode-change handshake and settling indication.

### Code
```systemverilog
timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
realtime previous_edge, interval_expected;
bit have_edge = 0;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
  if (!rst_n) have_edge = 0;
  else begin
    if (have_edge)
      assert ($realtime-previous_edge >= 0.95*interval_expected &&
              $realtime-previous_edge <= 1.05*interval_expected);
    previous_edge = $realtime;
    interval_expected = expected_clock_period;
    have_edge = 1;
  end
end
```

Comparing against the newest value at the end of an interval wrongly rejects a legal old-mode interval. Updating configuration in the same simulation region as this checker creates a race. | Sample | A | B | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | History |
| 1 | 1 | 0 | A changes |
| 2 | 1 | 0 | One cycle later |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | B changes: obligation met |

Consecutive A changes require B changes on consecutive corresponding samples. The rule requires a change at the target sample but does not prohibit B from changing earlier or at other times.

### Code
```systemverilog
bit past_valid = 0;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) past_valid <= 0;
  else past_valid <= 1;
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  past_valid && $changed(A) |-> ##2 $changed(B));
```

**Key idea:** A burst must remain inside its original 1 KB region, including every transferred byte of every accepted beat.

| Start | Beat bytes | Beats | Last byte | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x3f0 | 4 | 4 | 0x3ff | Legal |
| 0x3f4 | 4 | 4 | 0x403 | Illegal |

### Explanation
For a fixed-length incrementing burst, compute last_byte = start + beats*bytes_per_beat - 1 with widened unsigned arithmetic. Compare start and last_byte after shifting right by ten. For indefinite INCR bursts and wrapping bursts, track the actual accepted address sequence instead. Only accepted address phases advance the tracker: HREADY must be high and HTRANS must be NONSEQ or SEQ. BUSY and IDLE do not count as data beats.

### Code
```systemverilog
function automatic bit incr_fits_1k(
  input longint unsigned start,
  input int unsigned beats,
  input int unsigned bytes_per_beat);
  longint unsigned last_byte;
  if (beats == 0 || bytes_per_beat == 0) return 0;
  last_byte = start + longint'(beats)*bytes_per_beat - 1;
  if (last_byte < start) return 0; // arithmetic overflow
  return (start >> 10) == (last_byte >> 10);
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
This helper assumes legal aligned addresses and a known incrementing burst length; it is not a complete AHB monitor. Check HSIZE against bus width, alignment, HREADY stalls, and wrap-address calculation separately. Avoid counting the data phase as another accepted address.

### Follow-ups
For accepted SEQ beats, compare address[ADDR_W-1:10] with the NONSEQ start region and check the final byte's region too; retain state through BUSY cycles.

**Key idea:** $fell detects a sampled transition whose current least-significant bit is zero and whose previous bit was one, X, or Z.

| Previous sampled a | Current a | $fell(a) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |
| X | 0 | 1 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 0 |

### Explanation
For a known one-bit signal, the familiar case is 1→0. Four-state semantics also allow X/Z→0, so the source note describing only 1→0 is incomplete. The example requires b at the sample following a detected fall. A history flag avoids treating the first post-reset sample as a meaningful transition from an uninitialized historical value. For vectors, $fell examines the least-significant bit rather than detecting an arbitrary falling bit.

### Code
```systemverilog
bit have_history = 0;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) have_history <= 0;
  else have_history <= 1;
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  have_history && $fell(a) |=> b);
// Strict known 1-to-0 interpretation:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  have_history && ($past(a) === 1'b1) && (a === 1'b0) |=> b);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The two properties are alternatives for different contracts, not necessarily checks to enable together. A fall between clock samples can be missed. Check b for X explicitly if the diagnostic should distinguish unknown from false.

### Follow-ups
For a same-sample requirement use |-> b. For a response two cycles later use |-> ##2 b; do not accidentally add another cycle with |=> ##2.

**Key idea:** Immediate assertions check a procedural instant; concurrent assertions check sampled temporal behavior.

| Feature | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical syntax | assert(expr) | assert property(...) |
| Execution | When process reaches statement | On declared sampling event |
| Time relationship | Boolean now | Sequences across samples |

### Explanation
An immediate assertion is useful after a calculation or transaction comparison. It sees values available in its current scheduling region. A concurrent property samples signals at its clock event and evaluates temporal obligations using assertion scheduling rules. It can therefore express “request now implies acknowledgement next cycle” without manually saving history. Both kinds should have actionable diagnostics.

### Code
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  assert (!$isunknown(select)) else $error("Unknown select");
end
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 req |=> ack)
  else $error("Expected acknowledgement after request");
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
An immediate assert inside an always @(posedge clk) does not automatically gain concurrent assertion sampling semantics; it can observe pre-NBA values and race with blocking testbench drives. X/Z in a Boolean assertion expression is not true and causes failure. A temporal implication can pass vacuously when its trigger never occurs, so pair it with coverage.

Can an immediate assertion check a protocol? Yes, using explicitly maintained history/state; concurrent syntax normally makes the intended clock relationship clearer.

**Key idea:** Blocking assignment updates immediately; nonblocking assignment schedules the update after right-hand sides have been evaluated.

| Before edge | Statements | After NBA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a=1, b=0 | a <= b; b <= a; | a=0, b=1 |
| a=1, b=0 | a = b; b = a; | a=0, b=0 |

### Explanation
For a clocked register pipeline, each stage must capture the previous stage's old value on the same edge. Nonblocking assignments provide that behavior within and across clocked processes. Blocking assignments are appropriate for ordered combinational calculations where later statements intentionally use newly computed values. These conventions describe intended hardware and reduce races, but assignment choice alone does not resolve multiple writers.

### Code
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
  if (!rst_n) begin stage1 <= 0; stage2 <= 0; end
  else begin stage1 <= din; stage2 <= stage1; end
end
always_comb begin
  sum = a + b;
  result = sum ^ mask;
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
Do not drive the same variable from unrelated processes. A testbench that drives din with a blocking assignment at the active clock edge can race with the sequential block even though the DUT uses NBA. Use a clocking block or an agreed different drive edge. Combinational blocks need complete assignments to avoid latches.

### Follow-ups
Does NBA make execution parallel? RHS expressions still execute in processes; deferred updates make register sampling behave as simultaneous old-state capture.

**Key idea:** Choose the print task according to when values must be observed and whether a newline is needed.

| Task | Timing | Newline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $display | At execution | Yes |
| $write | At execution | No |
| $strobe | End of current time slot | Yes |
| $monitor | End of slot after monitored change | Yes |

### Explanation
Nonblocking updates are deferred, so a display immediately following an NBA normally sees the old value. A strobe in that same slot reports the final value after updates. monitor installs a change-driven reporting list; calling it again replaces the active list instead of adding an independent monitor. Use monitoron and monitoroff to control that list when needed.

### Code
```systemverilog
module prints;
  logic q = 0;
  initial begin
    $monitor("monitor q=%0b", q);
    #1;
    q <= 1;
    $display("display q=%0b", q); // 0
    $strobe("strobe q=%0b", q);   // 1
    $write("prefix: ");
    $display("message");
    #1 $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The relative order of multiple end-of-slot messages should not be treated as a protocol guarantee. Use $time or $realtime plus instance and transaction identifiers for useful diagnostics. A display in an assertion action can show current rather than sampled signal values; use $sampled when reporting the values checked by a concurrent property.

For printing a multi-part line use $write, but concurrent processes can interleave their output; build one string before logging when message integrity matters.

| Construct | Wildcards |
| --- | --- |
| case | None: X/Z match literally |
| casez | Z and ? |
| casex | X, Z and ? |

### Explanation
This four-request priority encoder assigns the highest index first and supplies complete defaults. It avoids wildcard interpretation entirely. With unknown request bits, ordinary if conditions may still choose a lower known request, so an independent known-value check is useful in verification. The valid flag distinguishes index zero selected from no request.

### Code
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  valid = 1'b1;
  index = 2'd0;
  if      (req[3]) index = 2'd3;
  else if (req[2]) index = 2'd2;
  else if (req[1]) index = 2'd1;
  else if (req[0]) index = 2'd0;
  else            valid = 1'b0;

assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)

```

| Event | Outstanding IDs |
| --- | --- |
| Issue ID 7 | 7 |
| Issue ID 2 | 7,2 |
| Receive ID 2 | 7 |
| Receive ID 7 | Empty |

### Explanation
The key must uniquely identify a live transaction. Store a value snapshot or clone of mutable objects so later producer edits cannot change the expectation. On a response, first check existence, then compare, report, and consume according to the scoreboard policy. This example consumes even a mismatching response after reporting it, avoiding a second misleading leftover error for an already completed transaction.

### Code
```systemverilog
class response_model;
  bit [31:0] expected[int unsigned];
  function void issue(int unsigned id, bit [31:0] data);
    if (expected.exists(id)) $error("Duplicate outstanding ID %0d", id);
    else expected[id] = data;
  endfunction
  function void receive(int unsigned id, bit [31:0] data);
    if (!expected.exists(id)) $error("Unexpected ID %0d", id);
```
